chapter: Opinions on pop music, jazz education and the business
title: Gimmick hits: Tiny Tim and Wee Bonnie Baker
summary: Wilson says a novelty like 'Tiptoe Through the Tulips' or 'Oh Johnny' can flare up and vanish, while real jazz endures.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Well, regardless of what he does, or she does, I do -- oh, jazz will exist forever. (simultaneous talk)

Another thing that helps to confuse what we're talking about, like we were talking about making a living, making money from this, and I was saying earlier about the rock movement going down in record sales. But you never know when gimmicks will come up, just like when Tiny Tim came up singing 'Tiptoe Through the Tulips,' in a falsetto voice, and he was the toast of the country with a gold record. See, all that kind of thing can happen. And you can't forsee that, can you? And old man singing 'Tiptoe Through The Tulips' in that high soprano voice, I mean, really! And he was the toast of the country.
I saw him in the subway before he got popular, and two months later ...
Steven never heard Tiny Tim singing 'Tiptoe Through The Tulips.'

You know, I saw him in the subway two months before he got popular with that, and he was dressed just the way he was -- and he might have been working on that tune, and two months later, he became the rage. I saw that guy on the subway and thought, that's just another freak, and then I see him on TV.
What he represents is part of this
business, too, though. Those are the kinds of things that come up.

I remember years ago, that song, a girl came up with, singing 'Oh Johnny', with Benny Goodman and Artie Shaw riding the crest -- that little girl came up--Wee Bonnie Baker-- came up singing 'Oh Johnny', and took over all the record sales for six weeks. Nobody was even talking about Benny Goodman while this girl was singing 'Oh Johnny', that song. But you see, those kinds of things happen in this business. 'The Music Goes Round and Round', the jazz world of the early thirties.

But those things, see, they flare up like a big rocket and they flare right down -- for six weeks or so, just like Tiny Tim, you know, and it's a temporary thing. It's hard to repeat; it's hard for Tiny Tim to establish a career doing that, that was a one time thing -- 'Tiptoe Through the Tulips'. It's not a solid thing like jazz is, real jazz or classical music, that carries you on, it never hits a giant sale like 'Tiptoe Through the Tulips.' No jazz record would ever sell like that, I guess, but it will go on and on and on, that's jazz. It doesn't die, as I said earlier, even though everybody is always so anxious to write its obituary.
